title: MANAGING LOCAL USERS AND GROUPS
display: Ch 6 — MANAGING LOCAL USERS AND GROUPS

content.text: Book reference: Chapter 6, pages 161–204. Guided Exercises: Gaining Superuser Access, Managing Local User Accounts, Managing Local Group Accounts, Managing User Passwords. Lab: Managing Local Users and Groups.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This whole chapter

Creating/modifying/deleting users and groups, granting sudo access, and setting password-aging policy are all standard, hands-on RHCSA tasks. This is one of the highest-yield chapters in the whole course.

Every process runs as some user, and every file is owned by some user — that ownership is the whole basis of Linux access control. Internally the system tracks a numeric UID, not the username; the name is just a friendly label mapped to that number.
Full access to the system, no restrictions
Run background services/daemons; not meant for interactive login

Before RHEL 7, the split was 1–499 system / 500+ regular. The current ranges (and everything else useradd defaults to) live in /etc/login.defs — editing that file only changes defaults for users created afterward, never retroactively.

id shows a user's UID, primary GID, and every group they belong to; id username checks someone else. ls -l shows a file's owning user in column 3; ls -ld does the same for a directory itself rather than its contents.
/etc/passwd — one line per user, seven colon-separated fields
Always x — the real encrypted password lives in /etc/shadow instead
Login shell — /sbin/nologin blocks interactive login for service accounts

Every user has exactly one primary group (the GID in /etc/passwd) — by default a private group auto-created with the same name as the user, containing only that user. That simplifies permission management, as you'll see in Chapter 7. A user can additionally belong to any number of supplementary groups, tracked in /etc/group; access is granted if ANY of a user's groups (primary or supplementary) has permission — there's no distinction once access is being checked.

Fields, left to right: group name, always x, GID, comma-separated list of supplementary members. (Someone's primary group doesn't appear in that member list — it's implied by their /etc/passwd entry instead.)
⚠ WARNING — Don't log in as root directly

Red Hat's guidance: log in as a normal user and escalate only when needed, via su or sudo. Running an entire desktop session as root means any compromised app has full system access — normal users escalating on demand contains the blast radius of anything that goes wrong.
Switch user, non-login shell — keeps your current environment
Switch user, login shell — sets up the environment fresh, as if that user had just logged in (the recommended form)
Run one command as root, authenticating with YOUR OWN password, not root's
Interactive root shell, root's own login environment
Interactive root shell via su - (widely used in this course's own examples for consistent PATH behavior)
💡 Why this matters — Why sudo instead of just su

su needs root's actual password — a problem if root's password is deliberately unset (common on cloud images) or if you don't want every admin to know it. sudo instead checks a policy file for what YOU, personally, are allowed to run, authenticated with your own password. That also means access can be granted or revoked per-person without ever sharing a shared secret.

Every sudo command is logged to /var/log/secure — who ran what, as whom, from where. An unauthorized attempt is refused, logged, and (by default) emailed to root — sudo -k or an unlisted user trying anyway produces "user is not in the sudoers file. This incident will be reported."

/etc/sudoers is the master config — edit it ONLY with visudo, which locks the file and syntax-checks it before saving, preventing a broken sudoers file from locking everyone out simultaneously. In this course (and in practice) it's cleaner to drop a small file into /etc/sudoers.d/ instead of editing the master file directly — its contents are automatically included.
# /etc/sudoers.d/admin — grant full sudo to everyone in the admin group
The leading % means "this is a group, not a user." The two ALLs mean "on any host" and "run any command as any user."

RHEL 7 and 8 automatically grant full sudo to every member of the wheel group. RHEL 6 did not. A site that repurposed the wheel group for something unrelated before upgrading could unintentionally hand out admin access system-wide — worth auditing group membership after any major-version upgrade.
Know every row of this table without needing to look it up.
Add to a supplementary group (keeps existing ones)
⚠ WARNING — usermod -G vs -aG — the single most common mistake

-G replaces a user's ENTIRE supplementary group list with whatever you specify — leave one out and they silently lose that membership. -a ("append") is what you almost always want when adding to an existing set: usermod -aG newgroup username. Forgetting -a is one of the most common real-world sudo/access-loss mistakes.
⚠ WARNING — userdel without -r leaves orphaned files

useradd assigns the next free UID ≥ 1000. If you delete a user without -r and later create a new one, that new user can be handed the old, now-unused UID — and silently inherit ownership of every file the old user left behind outside their home directory. root can hunt these down with find / -nouser -o -nogroup. Prefer userdel -r, or manually reassign orphaned files, to avoid this information-leakage risk entirely.
Create a system group (auto GID from system range)
A group can't be deleted while it's still someone's primary group — reassign that user's primary group first. And just like with users, check for files still owned by the old GID afterward.

Recommended practice: reserve a GID range clearly above 1000 for your own supplementary groups, since UIDs (and matching private-group GIDs) for regular users also start at 1000 — keeping ranges visually distinct avoids confusing collisions later.
/etc/shadow (readable only by root) holds the actual encrypted password plus aging data — nine colon-separated fields:
Encrypted password — format $id$salt$hash (6=SHA-512, the RHEL 8 default; 1=MD5; 5=SHA-256)
Days since 1970-01-01 the password was last changed
Minimum days before it can be changed again
Maximum days before it must be changed
Inactivity grace period after expiry before the account locks
💡 Why this matters — What the salt actually buys you

The salt is random per-user data mixed into the password before hashing. Without it, two users who both pick "redhat" would have identical /etc/shadow entries, making pattern-based cracking trivially easy across every account at once. With distinct salts, identical passwords hash to completely different strings — an attacker has to crack each account individually.
Display current aging settings for a user
Inactive days after expiry before lockout
Force a password change at next login
date -d "+180 days" +%F calculates a future date in the exact YYYY-MM-DD format chage -E expects — a handy combo instead of counting days by hand.

PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, and PASS_WARN_AGE in /etc/login.defs set the default policy applied to NEW users only — exactly like the UID range defaults, changing this file never touches existing accounts.
Blocks password authentication; can be reversed with -U
Blocks login entirely once the date passes
Account can still authenticate for non-shell services (mail, file transfer) but gets an immediate disconnect on interactive login attempts
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Locking out a departing employee

The recommended real-world pattern combines two of the above in one command: usermod -L -e 2019-10-05 username — locks the password immediately AND sets a hard expiration date. If the person returns, unlock with usermod -U and remember to also clear/update the expiration date.

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. ssh student@servera, sudo su - to get a root shell.
2. useradd operator1; passwd operator1 (set it to something like redhat123) — note the weak-password warning still lets root proceed.
3. usermod -c "Operator One" operator1; confirm with tail /etc/passwd.
4. groupadd -g 30000 operators; usermod -aG operators operator1; confirm with id operator1.
5. echo "%operators ALL=(ALL) ALL" > /etc/sudoers.d/operators, then su - operator1 and confirm sudo works for that account.
6. chage -M 90 -W 7 operator1; chage -l operator1 to confirm.
7. usermod -L operator1; try su - operator1 (should fail); usermod -U operator1 to restore it.

1. Q1 — You run usermod -G developers alice, intending to add her to the developers group. She reports she can no longer access files she used to reach through her other group memberships. What went wrong?
2. Q2 — Why does sudo ask for YOUR password rather than root's, and what file logs every command run through it?

3. Q3 — An employee leaves the company today, effective immediately. What single usermod command both blocks them right now and guarantees the account can't be reactivated by anyone forgetting to revisit it later?

Q1 — -G (uppercase, no -a) replaces the ENTIRE supplementary group list rather than adding to it — alice lost every group she wasn't re-listed in. The fix going forward is usermod -aG developers alice.

Q2 — sudo checks the policy in /etc/sudoers (and /etc/sudoers.d/) for what the person running it is individually permitted to do, authenticated against their own account — so access can be granted or revoked per person without anyone needing to know a shared root password. Every invocation logs to /var/log/secure.

Q3 — usermod -L -e $(date -d today +%F) username — locks the password immediately and sets the account's expiration to today, so even if someone forgets to follow up, the expiration date is already a hard stop.
Three account types: superuser (UID 0), system users (1–999), regular users (1000+); /etc/passwd and /etc/group map names to the UIDs/GIDs the system actually tracks.
Prefer su - (login shell, fresh environment) and sudo (per-user, own-password authentication, fully logged) over logging in directly as root.
useradd/usermod/userdel and groupadd/groupmod/groupdel are the core account-management toolkit; -aG (not -G) is how you add to, rather than replace, a user's supplementary groups.
/etc/shadow holds salted, hashed passwords plus aging data; chage manages that aging policy per user, while /etc/login.defs sets defaults for future users only.
usermod -L (lock), an expiration date (-e / chage -E), and /sbin/nologin are the three tools for restricting or ending an account's access.
